title: Equations with trigonometric functions can encode infinite computations

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Equations with trigonometric functions can encode infinite computations

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Whereas solving pure polynomial equations allows no computation beyond that of ordinary discrete systems, once trigonometric functions are allowed one can construct equations whose solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of infinitely many steps of a system like a cellular automaton.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: as soon as one even allows trigonometric functions, for example, it turns out that it becomes possible to construct equations for which finding a solution is equivalent to finding the outcome of an infinite number of steps in the evolution of a system like a cellular automaton.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “The Validity of the Principle” (from p. 726), pp. 731–732. Scope: equations built from standard mathematical functions

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-09: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.88

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Undecidability reductions for equations with periodic functions are finite mathematical objects and can be checked now. Careful domain restrictions are essential, but no new empirical observations are needed.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Check a reduction mapping an arbitrary infinite cellular-automaton evolution or halting instance to existence of a solution of an equation using integers, arithmetic, and trigonometric functions. Correct equivalence proves undecidability; a flaw in the encoding refutes the construction.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The statement depends on the exact equation language, domain, and meaning of 'finding a solution'.

The contrast with pure polynomial equations changes when integer rather than real solutions are allowed.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Both halves are existence and non-existence theorems about equations, not observations. Decidability results for real polynomial constraints, and Richardson's theorem for elementary functions with sine, are published and checkable. Turning the undecidability proof into an explicit cellular-automaton encoding is a finite logic exercise, which puts the claim within present methods even though the book does not spell every substitution out.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For polynomial equations, use decidability of the existential theory of the reals to show that solvability does not encode arbitrary cellular-automaton evolution. For trigonometric equations, give an explicit family whose solutions encode the state of a cellular automaton after arbitrarily many steps. Existence of that family confirms the trigonometric clause; a decision procedure for it would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Richardson's original class uses absolute value and exponentials together with sine, so the write-up must land in the trigonometric fragment named in the claim.

Encoding an arbitrary finite number of steps is weaker than a single equation that packages infinitely many steps, and the construction has to match the stronger reading.
